transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, hi. It's nice to meet you too, I guess. I mean, as nice as it can be under the circumstances. I didn't really want to come in, to be honest with you. I'm a manager over at the plant—have been for years—and I'm used to handling things on my own. You know, keeping the gears turning, making sure everyone else is doing what they're supposed to be doing. I never finished high school, had to drop out in the 8th grade to work, so I've always just put my head down and pushed through whatever was in front of me. But lately... lately, it's just been different. 

I've been feeling so heavy, like I'm just dragging myself through every single day. And the other night, well, I was sitting in my recliner after everyone went to bed, just staring at the wall, and I started thinking... I just kept having these thoughts that my family might be better off if I didn't wake up in the morning. Like, if my heart just stopped in my sleep, it would be a relief for them. Not that I'd do anything, mind you, but just... hoping for it. And it wasn't just a passing thought, it just sat there, heavy in my chest. It scared me, really scared me. I've never thought like that before. I was so shaken up the next day at work that I actually broke down and told my supervisor about it. He's a good guy, known him for twenty years, and he's the one who told me I needed to come see someone. So... here I am.
Did something specific happen before this started that you think brought it on?

Well, yeah, I suppose there was. If I really sit down and look at the calendar, I guess this whole change in me started right around the time my daughter left. It's been about two weeks now. Exactly two weeks, actually, come this Thursday. 

You see, she just shipped out for the military. Left Georgia to go off to basic training. And, you know, I’m proud of her, I really am. I’ve worked at the plant my whole life, busting my hump since I was just a kid so she’d have opportunities I never had, and seeing her step up to serve her country... it’s a big deal. A really big deal. We had this whole big send-off for her, all the aunts and uncles came over, and we made a big barbecue out back. Everybody was laughing and carrying on, giving her advice. 

But then... well, the morning she actually drove off, it just hit me like a freight train. The house was just dead quiet. I remember sitting at the kitchen table just staring at the grain in the wood, thinking about how far away she was going and how I couldn't protect her anymore. That’s really when this whole dark cloud, this heavy feeling I was telling you about, just settled right over me. So, yeah, it’s been going on for about two weeks, right since she left Georgia for the military. I keep telling myself it's just part of life, kids grow up and move on, but I just haven't been able to shake this off since she pulled out of that driveway.
Since your daughter left, have there still been moments when you could enjoy anything, even briefly?

Well, I... I wish I could say yes to that. I really do. You'd think a man could find at least a minute or two of peace, maybe just a brief second where things feel normal, but... no. Not really. 

I used to have all these things that kept me busy, things I actually looked forward to doing when I wasn't pulling shifts at the plant. Like my garden. I've always kept a real nice garden out back, and I used to be out there every single evening, just messing with my tomato plants. Checking the soil, picking off the bugs, tying up the vines so they don't snap when the fruit gets heavy. Or I'd be out in the garage. I got this old wood bench out there, and I’d just stand there and sand wood for hours. Didn't even have to be making anything special, just the feel of the wood getting smooth under my hands... it was relaxing, you know? 

And on Sundays, well, I’d always watch the Falcons play. I never missed a game, even when they were playing terrible and breaking my heart. And before that, at church, I was always the guy who stayed way after the service was over, just standing around talking to folks in the fellowship hall, catching up on everyone's week and drinking that awful coffee they make. 

But lately? Since she drove off? I just... I look at all that stuff, the garden, the workbench, the football games, and it's like it all belongs to somebody else. I walk right past the tomatoes and I don't even care if they're dying on the vine. I haven't turned on the TV for a game, haven't picked up a piece of sandpaper, and at church, I just slip out the back door as soon as the preacher says amen. It’s like the color just drained right out of every single thing I used to care about. I try to force myself, I tell myself, "Go out to the garage, just for ten minutes," but the want-to... it’s just completely gone.
Before your daughter left, had you ever gone through another period like this?

Well, if I'm being completely honest with you... and I guess that's why I'm sitting in this chair, right? If I really sit down and look back at it, yeah. I have. 

It's not something I like to admit, especially not to myself. Like I was saying earlier, I'm the guy who keeps the gears turning at the plant. People look at me and they expect steady. They expect a guy who doesn't get rattled, a guy who always knows what to do when a machine goes down or a shipment is late. So when I started feeling... off... I just pushed it down. I figured it was just part of getting older. But looking back on it now, really taking a hard look at things, these... these low stretches, they’ve actually been coming around for about a year now. 

I remember last fall, right around the time we were doing the big annual inventory at the plant—which is always a complete nightmare, let me tell you, trying to count every single bolt and bracket—I started getting that same heavy feeling. I just chalked it up to being tired, you know? Working fifty-hour weeks on concrete floors since I was a teenager, I just figured my body and my brain were telling me I needed a vacation I was never gonna take. I’d go through these spells where I just didn't want to deal with the paperwork, didn't want to answer the radio, just wanted to go home and sit in my recliner in the dark. And then, eventually, it would kind of lift for a bit, and I'd think, "Alright, you're fine, you just needed a weekend to catch your breath, back to work." 

So, yeah, it’s been happening off and on for about a solid year. Just these stretches where everything feels like you're trying to walk through wet cement. But I'll tell you this... none of those other times were anything like what I'm going through right now. Not even close. Those were just... dips, I guess. Annoying, but I could still push through 'em. But this one? This one right here after my daughter left for basic? It has hit me the absolute hardest. It’s like those other times were just a little rain shower, and this is a category five hurricane just sitting right over my house and refusing to move. I just... I've never felt it go this deep before.
Before this current episode, was there ever a time when you felt depressed or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

Well, let me think about that. You're asking if any of those other low stretches lasted a solid two weeks, every single day... I guess... well, it's hard to say for sure. 

Like I said, I'm a working man. I've been managing the floor at that plant for a long time, and you don't really get to just stop and take a mental health day, you know? You just keep putting one foot in front of the other because you've got a crew relying on you. So when I felt those dips coming on, like back during that inventory I mentioned, I just kept my head down. I didn't really keep track of the days on a calendar or anything like that. 

I mean, I know there were times I felt real heavy and didn't want to be bothered with anything, but did it last exactly two weeks straight without a break? Every single day? I honestly couldn't tell you. It might have been a week, might have been ten days, might have been that I'd feel terrible Monday through Thursday, and then maybe Friday I'd feel a little lighter because the weekend was coming, even though I usually end up working Saturdays anyway. It all kind of blurs together when you're just trying to survive the shift and get home to your recliner. 

So, I don't know. I can't sit here and swear to you that any of those previous times lasted a full two weeks of just pure misery every single day. Not like this time. This time, since she left, I know exactly how many days it's been because I've felt every single minute of it. But those other times? I just don't have a clear enough memory of the exact timeline to give you a straight yes or no on that. It was just... it was just a general feeling of being worn down and not caring, but I couldn't put a stopwatch to it, if you know what I mean.
Because of how you've been feeling these past two weeks, have you been unable to do your job or take care of things at home?

Well... yeah. That’s... that's the hard truth of it, and I'll tell you, it ain't easy for a man like me to admit. 

You see, at the plant, I'm supposed to be the one keeping the wheels on the wagon. I'm the guy who catches the errors, double-checks the shift logs, makes sure the lines keep running. But these last couple weeks... I've been messing up. And not just little slip-ups, either. I'm talking serious mistakes that really mess up the workflow. It got so bad that... well, the other morning, I pulled into the lot before dawn, like I always do. It was still pitch black out, and I parked my truck in my usual spot right by the fence. But I just... I couldn't turn the engine off. I couldn't open the door to get out. I just sat there gripping the steering wheel, staring at the building, feeling like I couldn't breathe. 

I must've sat out there for a good hour with the engine idling. My supervisor, he noticed my truck was out there but saw I hadn't clocked in, so he actually came out into the cold and tapped on my window. He took one look at me—just sitting there in the dark, completely frozen up—and he ended up getting occupational health involved. They made it this whole official thing, which, let me tell you, is humiliating. Me, the manager, having to go sit with the occupational health nurse because I can't even walk through the front doors of my own workplace. 

And then I come home, and it ain't a bit better. I've always been a pay-on-time kind of guy, you know? You get a bill, you write the check that same evening, put a stamp on it, and it goes in the box the next morning. That's just how you handle your business. But right now? I walk in the door and I just drop the mail on the kitchen counter. There's a pile there right now that just keeps growing. Bills, letters, all the responsibilities I'm supposed to be taking care of... I’ve just let them pile up instead of handling them like I normally would. I look at that stack every day, and I know the electric company doesn't care about my problems, I know I need to open them, but I just walk right past it and go sit in my chair. It's like I'm just watching my whole life fall apart and I can't even lift a finger to stop it.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don’t seem to?

Well, no... no, doc, I ain't... I'm not going crazy, if that's what you're asking. I know sometimes people get so far down in the hole they start imagining things, but it's not like that for me. It's actually almost the exact opposite, if I'm being honest. It's just quiet. Too quiet. Like when I'm sitting in that recliner I told you about, with all that mail piling up on the counter in the other room... it's just me and my own thoughts. 

Now, my thoughts are loud enough, let me tell you. Just churning and churning over all the mistakes I've been making at the plant, and worrying about my daughter out there at basic, hoping she's doing alright and keeping her boots shined and all that. But I'm not hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there or anything out of a movie. 

I remember this one guy on my crew, years and years ago, maybe back in '98 or '99... he worked the stamping press. Good guy, hard worker, but he started talking to people who weren't there. We had to get him off the floor for his own safety. You just can't have a guy losing his grip on reality around heavy machinery, it's a recipe for a lost limb or worse. But me? No, I'm fully aware of what's real and what's not. I see the bills I'm ignoring, I hear the refrigerator humming in the kitchen, I see the dust gathering on the TV stand. It's all just the normal, everyday stuff. It's just that all that normal stuff feels like it weighs a thousand pounds right now. So, no... no visions or voices or anything like that. Just my own tired brain making me miserable.
Thinking about those earlier low periods over the past year, was there ever one that lasted at least two weeks?

Well, doc, like I was just trying to explain a minute or two ago... it's tough to put a real exact number of days on those older ones. I mean, looking back on it now, I can see that these low stretches, these dips where I just feel heavy and worn out, they've been coming around for about a year now. It started maybe last spring or summer, just creeping up on me here and there. I'd have a bad spell, push my way through it at the plant because I had to, and then maybe it would lift a bit. 

So did any of those specific stretches go for a full fourteen days straight without a single break? I really, honestly couldn't swear to it in a court of law. It's just a blur of shifts and weekends. But what I do know, what I can tell you for an absolute fact, is that this current one... this one right now, after my daughter packed up and left for basic... this one has hit me the absolute hardest. 

It's like night and day compared to those other times over the past year. Those other times were like driving with a flat tire, you know? You can still rumble along the shoulder if you really have to, even if it messes up the rim, and you just keep going. But this time? Since she left? It's like the whole engine just fell right out of the truck onto the highway. I just don't have anything left to keep it moving. So yeah, those low periods have been coming around for a year or so, but nothing—and I mean nothing—like this one right now.
Do you feel the way you've been feeling is stronger than what you'd expect from your daughter leaving for basic training?

Well... that's a tough one to answer, doc. I mean, it's my little girl, you know? My only kid. And basic training... it ain't summer camp. I was in the service myself, back in the day, so I know exactly what they're putting her through down there. The yelling, the physical strain, the lack of sleep, breaking you down to build you back up... I know it all. And as a father, you naturally worry. You sit there in your chair and you think, 'Is she eating enough? Is she keeping her head down? Is some drill sergeant riding her too hard?' So, yeah, it's normal to feel down, to feel anxious about it. Any parent worth their salt would be. 

But... I don't know. I've sent guys off to the military from the plant before. Young kids who worked the line for a year or two before signing up. I've always been proud of them, always shook their hands and wished them well. And yeah, I missed them around the shop, but it didn't stop me from doing my job. It didn't make me freeze up in my truck in the dark. 

And my wife, God rest her soul, she passed about five years back. Now that... that was a grief that just hollows you out. I remember feeling like I was walking underwater for months. But even then, even with that kind of loss, I still managed to pay the electric bill. I still managed to walk through those factory doors and do what needed doing. 

So, is this stronger than what you'd expect? I... I really couldn't say for sure. Maybe it's just the straw that broke the camel's back, you know? Maybe it's just all these years of keeping the wheels on the wagon finally catching up to me, and her leaving just knocked the last prop out from under me. I mean, it feels awful heavy, heavier than it probably should, but I just don't know what's normal anymore. I just know I'm sitting here talking to you instead of being on the floor making sure the shift is running right, and that... that just ain't right.
Have other people noticed that you’ve been moving or talking much slower than usual lately?

Well, doc, that's... yeah. Yeah, they have. It's actually been getting a bit embarrassing, to tell you the truth. I mean, I'm the operations manager, right? I'm supposed to be the guy keeping the pace, setting the tempo for the whole floor. If I'm dragging, the whole line drags, and we can't have that with the quotas we've got this quarter. But lately... man, it's like I'm moving through thick mud. Just getting from the office down to the stamping presses feels like a marathon. 

And the guys on the floor, they don't miss a trick. They're good guys, observant. A couple of the shift foremen—Jimmy, especially, he's been with me since '05—he actually pulled me aside by the breakroom the other day. Asked me point-blank if I was coming down with something, maybe that flu that's been going around the county. He said I was just... walking different. Slower. Like I had lead in my boots. 

And it ain't just the walking, either. It's the talking. Someone will come up to me with a clipboard, just a simple question about a parts requisition or a scheduling conflict—stuff I used to handle in my sleep, just snap-snap-snap, decision made. But now? They ask me, and I just stand there staring at them for what feels like a full minute. My brain is just... it's like a rusty gear that won't turn. I'm trying to pull the words together, but they just won't come out right away. I'm taking forever just to say 'yes' or 'no' or 'check with receiving.' 

So, yeah, they've noticed. They keep asking if I need to go home, if I need to see a doctor for a bug or something. They think I'm physically sick because I'm just... I'm just so bogged down, moving at half speed. It's frustrating, doc. I've always been a guy who gets things done, quick and efficient, and now I feel like I'm holding everyone up just by trying to put one foot in front of the other.
Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or high and needed much less sleep?

Energized? You know, it’s funny you ask that, doc, because... well, if you look at me right now, I know I look like a deflated tire. But just before this whole heavy, low spell hit me—right around the time before my girl packed her bags for basic—it was a completely different story. It was like night and day, really. 

I had this stretch where I was just... I don't know, feeling way too fired up. Like my engine was running hot and everything was finally going my way for once. We had this massive parts order come in from up in Detroit, the kind of order that usually makes the front office sweat bullets and panic about overtime. But me? I was looking at the floor plans and the shift schedules, and I just felt invincible. I was buzzing around the plant, thinking, 'I got this, this is my time, we're gonna absolutely crush these quotas.' I was just so fired up, feeling like I could tackle the work of ten men without even breaking a sweat. 

But... the thing is, doc, it wasn't just all high-fives and getting things done. There was this whole other side to it. Because I was running so hot, I was also... well, I was snapping at folks left and right. Just jumping down people's throats over the smallest, dumbest things that I normally just let slide without a second thought. 

Like Jimmy—I mentioned Jimmy earlier, my foreman who's been with me forever. He left a pallet jack parked maybe six inches outside the yellow safety lines near the loading dock. Six inches! Normally, I’d just nudge it with my boot or say, 'Hey Jim, square that up, would ya?' But that week? Man, I completely tore into him. I mean, I chewed him out up one side and down the other in front of half the day shift. Over a pallet jack! My blood was just boiling over absolutely nothing. It was like I had all this electricity pumping through me, and it either made me feel like the king of the factory or made me want to bite somebody's head off if they didn't move fast enough for me. So yeah, right before I crashed into this mud I'm in now, I was definitely way up there, just totally fired up or totally ticked off.
About that fired-up spell before your daughter left, did it last at least 4 days?

Four days? Well... shoot, doc, let me really think about that for a second. Because when you're running that hot, time just... it gets all warped, you know? 

See, the big Detroit order, the one I was telling you about, that hit my desk on a Tuesday. I remember because Tuesdays are when we do the weekly inventory counts, and I was already looking at the clipboards when the front office called down. So that was Tuesday. And my girl, she was shipping out that Sunday morning. We had to have her down at the processing station by 0600. 

So between that Tuesday and that Sunday... man, it's just a blur. I mean, when you're buzzing like that, and you're not really sleeping much, the days don't really have a hard stop and start. It just feels like one long, continuous shift. I'd be at the plant till all hours, come home, pace around the kitchen while she was packing her duffel bags, maybe close my eyes in the recliner for a bit, and then boom, I'm back at the factory before the sun's even thinking about coming up. 

So... was it four days exactly? Three days? Five? I honestly couldn't swear to it on a stack of Bibles. It might have been that whole week, or maybe just a few really intense days right in the middle there where I chewed Jimmy out. I just know it was a solid stretch where my foot was pushed all the way down on the gas pedal, right up until we dropped her off and the tank just... went completely empty. But pinning down the exact number of days? I just couldn't give you a straight answer on that. It's all just one big, fast, buzzing memory.
During that fired-up spell, did you need much less sleep than usual and still feel full of energy?

Sleep... well, see, that's... that's a tricky thing to answer, doc. Did I *need* less sleep? I honestly couldn't tell you. 

Like I was saying about that recliner in the living room—it's this old brown La-Z-Boy, had it since the kids were still in grade school—I was definitely spending a lot of time sitting in it that week instead of going up to bed. I'd be sitting there in the dark, listening to my girl rustling around upstairs with her duffel bags, checking her military packing list for the hundredth time. And my brain would just be going a mile a minute about the stamping presses and the Detroit order and the shipping manifests. 

But I don't really know if I was functioning on less sleep because I didn't *need* it, or if I just couldn't sleep because there was too much on my plate, you know? Normally, I'm a solid eight-hours guy. Head hits the pillow at 10 PM, out like a light, alarm goes off at 6 AM, regular as clockwork. But that week... I just don't know. 

And as for feeling full of energy while running on empty... again, I'm just not sure. I was awake, sure, and I was moving fast at the plant, but I was also drinking so much of that awful breakroom coffee. Jimmy makes it, and I swear to you it tastes like half-used motor oil, but I was gulping it down all day long. So maybe it was just the caffeine keeping me propped up, or maybe it was just pure adrenaline from the quotas and the stress of my little girl shipping out. 

So, to say I actually needed less sleep and felt energized from it... I just don't know if I can say yes to that. I was up, and my motor was running hot, but I can't rightly tell you if I actually had more natural energy or if my body was just completely refusing to shut down. It's hard to separate it all out.
During that fired-up spell, were you talking more than usual?

Talking more? Well... see, doc, that's another one of those things where I just... I really couldn't say for sure. 

Because if you think about it, my job... I mean, when you're running the floor, you're always talking anyway. You have to. You got the heavy stamping presses going, and those things, let me tell you, they put out this god-awful racket. Just a constant heavy metal slamming sound all day long. So if you want anybody to hear a single word you're saying, you're already practically yelling just to be heard over the machinery. I'm always on the walkie-talkie with the front office, or I'm barking at the forklift drivers to clear a lane, or I'm going over the clipboards with Jimmy. 

So that week with the big Detroit order, sure, I was giving orders. I was telling folks where to stage the materials and double-checking the shipping manifests so we didn't fall behind. But was I talking *more* than I usually do? I honestly haven't got a clue. Maybe I was talking faster, or maybe just a bit louder, like when I completely lost my temper with Jimmy over that pallet jack. I definitely gave him an earful then, chewed on him for a good five minutes straight. But overall for the whole week? I don't know if the actual amount of talking was any higher than a normal busy shift.

And then you look at how things were at home... my girl, when she’s focused, she gets this absolute tunnel vision. She was up in her room or down in the living room with all her gear spread out everywhere, checking off that military packing list they give them. And they have all these crazy rules for basic, you know? Like how to fold the t-shirts exactly right, how to roll the socks up so they look like little green sausages... it’s a whole strict process. So she didn't want to chat. She was stressed out about getting it right. 

I was mostly just sitting there in that brown recliner, watching her, maybe offering a piece of dad advice here and there about keeping her head down and just doing what the drill sergeants tell her. But I wasn't just sitting there talking her ear off about the factory or anything. My brain was going a mile a minute, sure, thinking about a hundred different things at once, but I was keeping a lot of it locked up in my own head. So... no, I don't think I was blabbering on more than usual. Or if I was, nobody at the plant or at home pointed it out to me.
During that fired-up spell, were you more driven than usual to start or do a lot of projects or work?

Projects? Oh... oh yeah, doc. That's... well, that's actually a big part of what made that whole week such a blur. The drive... it was like a fire in my belly that just wouldn't go out. 

See, normally, I leave the plant, I leave the work at the plant. I'm a manager, sure, but I'm not the owner. But that week with the Detroit order... I just couldn't turn it off. I was coming home, and instead of just sitting in the recliner like I said, I was... I was calling the shift supervisors. At home. After hours. I mean, poor Tommy, he was probably trying to eat dinner with his kids, and I'm on the phone with him at 8 PM, practically shouting about how we need to reroute the staging area for the pallets. 

And it wasn't just the phone calls. I was sitting at the kitchen table, pushing my daughter's duffel bags aside, and I was drawing up these entirely new work plans. I had these big sheets of graph paper—I don't even know where I found them, probably left over from when the kids were in high school—and I was mapping out the whole factory floor. I was convinced I had figured out a way to shave ten seconds off the stamping cycle. Ten seconds! In my head, it was the most important thing in the world right then. 

And then, if you can believe it, right in the middle of all this factory planning and my girl getting ready to ship out for basic... I decided it was the perfect time to fix the back deck. I've been meaning to replace those rotting boards by the stairs for three years. Three years! But suddenly, at like... I don't know, 6 AM on a Thursday, before I even went to the plant, I'm out there with a crowbar, ripping up the wood. My wife came out in her bathrobe, looking at me like I'd grown a second head, asking what on earth I was doing. 

But I just felt like... I don't know how to explain it, doc. It was like every single idea that popped into my head, whether it was the factory layout or the deck or whatever, it just had to be handled right then and there. There was no "I'll do this tomorrow." It was all "I have to do this right now, this very second." I was just completely driven, you know? Like I couldn't stop starting things even if I tried.
During that fired-up spell, did it cause serious problems at work or at home?

Serious problems? Well... I guess that really depends on what you consider a serious problem, doc. Because when you say "serious," I'm thinking, you know, did I get fired? Did my wife pack her bags and leave me? And the answer to that is no. Nothing like that happened, I can tell you that for sure. 

I mean, take the plant, for example. Like I told you, I was calling Tommy at all hours of the night, and I really chewed Jimmy out over that pallet jack. And Jimmy, he’s a good guy, he’s been with the company for... gosh, it’s got to be fifteen years now. Started out sweeping the loading dock and worked his way up. He’s got two kids in high school, so I know he needs the job, and I did feel a little bad about yelling at him the way I did. I really let him have it, up one side and down the other. But did it cause a serious problem? Not really. He actually brought me a coffee the next week—one of those awful motor oil ones—and we smoothed it over. He knows how the stress gets when the quotas are tight. And as for the work itself, we actually got that big Detroit order out on time. Beat the deadline by half a shift, actually. The front office was thrilled, even if the guys on the floor were probably calling me every name in the book behind my back. So at work... no, no real damage done.

And at home... well, my wife, she’s an absolute saint. Thirty-two years we’ve been married this October. She’s used to me being a bit bullheaded. When I was out there tearing up the deck boards at six in the morning with that crowbar, yeah, she was standing there on the porch in her pink terrycloth bathrobe just shaking her head at me. She told me I was acting like a damn fool and to keep the noise down before the Hendersons next door called the cops on us. But we didn't get into a big blowout fight over it or anything. She just sighed and went back inside to make breakfast. 

And my daughter, like I said, she was just so dialed into that military packing list, she barely even noticed I was acting any different. She was in her own world with the duffel bags. 

So... no. I wouldn't say there were any serious problems. It was a chaotic week, sure, and I was definitely running everybody a little ragged, myself included. I mean, half that deck is still torn up right now, just sitting under a blue plastic tarp because I ran out of steam on it. But we all just kind of got through it. I didn't ruin anything or break anything that can't be fixed, if that's what you're asking.
During that fired-up period, were you hospitalized or forced to stop working because of how you were acting?

Hospitalized? Oh, Lord, no. No, no, no. I haven't been in a hospital since... well, since my wife had our girl, and obviously I was just there pacing the waiting room for that one. I really don't hold with hospitals unless you've got a bone sticking out of your leg or you're bleeding out, you know? And even then, I'd probably just try to wrap it up with some duct tape and finish my shift. 

And forced to stop working? Doc, I don't think you quite get how things run down at the plant. If I stop working, the whole operation goes belly up. I'm the guy keeping all those plates spinning. Like I was saying about that big Detroit order... if I had just up and walked out, or if the front office had come down and told me to take a hike because I was acting too fired up, we would have missed that shipping deadline. Period. And if we lose that account, then guys like Jimmy are out of a job, and I'm not about to let that happen. 

I've been working since I was a kid, you know. Left school back in the eighth grade to pull my weight for my folks, and I haven't stopped grinding since. It's just what you do. I'm supposed to be the guy keeping the pace, setting the tempo for the whole floor. If I'm dragging, the whole line drags, and we can't have that with the quotas we've got this quarter. But lately... man, it's like I'm moving through thick mud. Just getting from the office down to the stamping presses feels like a marathon. 

And the guys on the floor, they don't miss a trick. They're good guys, observant. A couple of the shift foremen—Jimmy, especially, he's been with me since '05—he actually pulled me aside by the breakroom the other day. Asked me point-blank if I was coming down with something, maybe that flu that's been going around the county. He said I was just... walking different. Slower. Like I had lead in my boots. 

And it ain't just the walking, either. It's the talking. Someone will come up to me with a clipboard, just a simple question about a parts requisition or a scheduling conflict—stuff I used to handle in my sleep, just snap-snap-snap, decision made. But now? They ask me, and I just stand there staring at them for what feels like a full minute. My brain is just... it's like a rusty gear that won't turn. I'm trying to pull the words together, but they just won't come out right away. I'm taking forever just to say 'yes' or 'no' or 'check with receiving.' 

So, yeah, they've noticed. They keep asking if I need to go home, if I need to see a doctor for a bug or something. They think I'm physically sick because I'm just... I'm just so bogged down, moving at half speed. It's frustrating, doc. I've always been a guy who gets things done, quick and efficient, and now I feel like I'm holding everyone up just by trying to put one foot in front of the other.

doctor.intent: Determine whether he has had any lifetime manic or hypomanic episode, which would shift diagnosis away from unipolar depressive/adjustment disorders.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or high and needed much less sleep?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Before this low spell hit, I was either feeling way too fired up like everything was finally going my way or snapping at folks over small things I normally let slide.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of feeling unusually 'high' or 'energized', which corresponds to an elevated mood, a hallmark of hypomanic or manic episodes.

patient.answer:
Energized? You know, it’s funny you ask that, doc, because... well, if you look at me right now, I know I look like a deflated tire. But just before this whole heavy, low spell hit me—right around the time before my girl packed her bags for basic—it was a completely different story. It was like night and day, really. 

I had this stretch where I was just... I don't know, feeling way too fired up. Like my engine was running hot and everything was finally going my way for once. We had this massive parts order come in from up in Detroit, the kind of order that usually makes the front office sweat bullets and panic about overtime. But me? I was looking at the floor plans and the shift schedules, and I just felt invincible. I was buzzing around the plant, thinking, 'I got this, this is my time, we're gonna absolutely crush these quotas.' I was just so fired up, feeling like I could tackle the work of ten men without even breaking a sweat. 

But... the thing is, doc, it wasn't just all high-fives and getting things done. There was this whole other side to it. Because I was running so hot, I was also... well, I was snapping at folks left and right. Just jumping down people's throats over the smallest, dumbest things that I normally just let slide without a second thought. 

Like Jimmy—I mentioned Jimmy earlier, my foreman who's been with me forever. He left a pallet jack parked maybe six inches outside the yellow safety lines near the loading dock. Six inches! Normally, I’d just nudge it with my boot or say, 'Hey Jim, square that up, would ya?' But that week? Man, I completely tore into him. I mean, I chewed him out up one side and down the other in front of half the day shift. Over a pallet jack! My blood was just boiling over absolutely nothing. It was like I had all this electricity pumping through me, and it either made me feel like the king of the factory or made me want to bite somebody's head off if they didn't move fast enough for me. So yeah, right before I crashed into this mud I'm in now, I was definitely way up there, just totally fired up or totally ticked off.

inference.note: New history of a distinct pre-depressive period of abnormally increased energy with marked irritability suggests possible bipolar spectrum illness, so bipolar candidates are added. Adjustment disorder candidates are less likely given severity, suicidality, psychomotor slowing, functional impairment, and evidence of recurrent mood episodes beyond the immediate stressor.

doctor.question: About that fired-up spell before your daughter left, did it last at least 4 days?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the elevated/irritable mood (hypomanic) episode, which is not specified in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Four days? Well... shoot, doc, let me really think about that for a second. Because when you're running that hot, time just... it gets all warped, you know? 

See, the big Detroit order, the one I was telling you about, that hit my desk on a Tuesday. I remember because Tuesdays are when we do the weekly inventory counts, and I was already looking at the clipboards when the front office called down. So that was Tuesday. And my girl, she was shipping out that Sunday morning. We had to have her down at the processing station by 0600. 

So between that Tuesday and that Sunday... man, it's just a blur. I mean, when you're buzzing like that, and you're not really sleeping much, the days don't really have a hard stop and start. It just feels like one long, continuous shift. I'd be at the plant till all hours, come home, pace around the kitchen while she was packing her duffel bags, maybe close my eyes in the recliner for a bit, and then boom, I'm back at the factory before the sun's even thinking about coming up. 

So... was it four days exactly? Three days? Five? I honestly couldn't swear to it on a stack of Bibles. It might have been that whole week, or maybe just a few really intense days right in the middle there where I chewed Jimmy out. I just know it was a solid stretch where my foot was pushed all the way down on the gas pedal, right up until we dropped her off and the tank just... went completely empty. But pinning down the exact number of days? I just couldn't give you a straight answer on that. It's all just one big, fast, buzzing memory.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the recent elevated/irritable spell included decreased need for sleep, which would strongly support a bipolar spectrum diagnosis over unipolar depression.
doctor.question: During that fired-up spell, did you need much less sleep than usual and still feel full of energy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a decreased need for sleep during the manic/hypomanic episode, which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Sleep... well, see, that's... that's a tricky thing to answer, doc. Did I *need* less sleep? I honestly couldn't tell you. 

Like I was saying about that recliner in the living room—it's this old brown La-Z-Boy, had it since the kids were still in grade school—I was definitely spending a lot of time sitting in it that week instead of going up to bed. I'd be sitting there in the dark, listening to my girl rustling around upstairs with her duffel bags, checking her military packing list for the hundredth time. And my brain would just be going a mile a minute about the stamping presses and the Detroit order and the shipping manifests. 

But I don't really know if I was functioning on less sleep because I didn't *need* it, or if I just couldn't sleep because there was too much on my plate, you know? Normally, I'm a solid eight-hours guy. Head hits the pillow at 10 PM, out like a light, alarm goes off at 6 AM, regular as clockwork. But that week... I just don't know. 

And as for feeling full of energy while running on empty... again, I'm just not sure. I was awake, sure, and I was moving fast at the plant, but I was also drinking so much of that awful breakroom coffee. Jimmy makes it, and I swear to you it tastes like half-used motor oil, but I was gulping it down all day long. So maybe it was just the caffeine keeping me propped up, or maybe it was just pure adrenaline from the quotas and the stress of my little girl shipping out. 

So, to say I actually needed less sleep and felt energized from it... I just don't know if I can say yes to that. I was up, and my motor was running hot, but I can't rightly tell you if I actually had more natural energy or if my body was just completely refusing to shut down. It's hard to separate it all out.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior elevated/irritable period included abnormally increased talkativeness, which would help establish a hypomanic/manic episode and distinguish bipolar disorder from unipolar major depression.
doctor.question: During that fired-up spell, were you talking more than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about increased talkativeness or pressure to keep talking, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Talking more? Well... see, doc, that's another one of those things where I just... I really couldn't say for sure. 

Because if you think about it, my job... I mean, when you're running the floor, you're always talking anyway. You have to. You got the heavy stamping presses going, and those things, let me tell you, they put out this god-awful racket. Just a constant heavy metal slamming sound all day long. So if you want anybody to hear a single word you're saying, you're already practically yelling just to be heard over the machinery. I'm always on the walkie-talkie with the front office, or I'm barking at the forklift drivers to clear a lane, or I'm going over the clipboards with Jimmy. 

So that week with the big Detroit order, sure, I was giving orders. I was telling folks where to stage the materials and double-checking the shipping manifests so we didn't fall behind. But was I talking *more* than I usually do? I honestly haven't got a clue. Maybe I was talking faster, or maybe just a bit louder, like when I completely lost my temper with Jimmy over that pallet jack. I definitely gave him an earful then, chewed on him for a good five minutes straight. But overall for the whole week? I don't know if the actual amount of talking was any higher than a normal busy shift.

And then you look at how things were at home... my girl, when she’s focused, she gets this absolute tunnel vision. She was up in her room or down in the living room with all her gear spread out everywhere, checking off that military packing list they give them. And they have all these crazy rules for basic, you know? Like how to fold the t-shirts exactly right, how to roll the socks up so they look like little green sausages... it’s a whole strict process. So she didn't want to chat. She was stressed out about getting it right. 

I was mostly just sitting there in that brown recliner, watching her, maybe offering a piece of dad advice here and there about keeping her head down and just doing what the drill sergeants tell her. But I wasn't just sitting there talking her ear off about the factory or anything. My brain was going a mile a minute, sure, thinking about a hundred different things at once, but I was keeping a lot of it locked up in my own head. So... no, I don't think I was blabbering on more than usual. Or if I was, nobody at the plant or at home pointed it out to me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fired-up period included increased goal-directed activity, which would support a hypomanic/manic episode and help distinguish bipolar disorder from recurrent or single-episode major depression.
doctor.question: During that fired-up spell, were you more driven than usual to start or do a lot of projects or work?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I was calling supervisors after hours, drawing up new work plans, and starting home projects all at once like every idea had to be handled right then.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I was more driven to start or do a lot of projects or work during the elevated period, which corresponds to increased goal-directed activity.

patient.answer:
Projects? Oh... oh yeah, doc. That's... well, that's actually a big part of what made that whole week such a blur. The drive... it was like a fire in my belly that just wouldn't go out. 

See, normally, I leave the plant, I leave the work at the plant. I'm a manager, sure, but I'm not the owner. But that week with the Detroit order... I just couldn't turn it off. I was coming home, and instead of just sitting in the recliner like I said, I was... I was calling the shift supervisors. At home. After hours. I mean, poor Tommy, he was probably trying to eat dinner with his kids, and I'm on the phone with him at 8 PM, practically shouting about how we need to reroute the staging area for the pallets. 

And it wasn't just the phone calls. I was sitting at the kitchen table, pushing my daughter's duffel bags aside, and I was drawing up these entirely new work plans. I had these big sheets of graph paper—I don't even know where I found them, probably left over from when the kids were in high school—and I was mapping out the whole factory floor. I was convinced I had figured out a way to shave ten seconds off the stamping cycle. Ten seconds! In my head, it was the most important thing in the world right then. 

And then, if you can believe it, right in the middle of all this factory planning and my girl getting ready to ship out for basic... I decided it was the perfect time to fix the back deck. I've been meaning to replace those rotting boards by the stairs for three years. Three years! But suddenly, at like... I don't know, 6 AM on a Thursday, before I even went to the plant, I'm out there with a crowbar, ripping up the wood. My wife came out in her bathrobe, looking at me like I'd grown a second head, asking what on earth I was doing. 

But I just felt like... I don't know how to explain it, doc. It was like every single idea that popped into my head, whether it was the factory layout or the deck or whatever, it just had to be handled right then and there. There was no "I'll do this tomorrow." It was all "I have to do this right now, this very second." I was just completely driven, you know? Like I couldn't stop starting things even if I tried.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior energized/irritable episode caused observable impairment, which would help distinguish hypomania from mania and narrow bipolar II vs bipolar I/unspecified bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: During that fired-up spell, did it cause serious problems at work or at home?

patient.answer:
Serious problems? Well... I guess that really depends on what you consider a serious problem, doc. Because when you say "serious," I'm thinking, you know, did I get fired? Did my wife pack her bags and leave me? And the answer to that is no. Nothing like that happened, I can tell you that for sure. 

I mean, take the plant, for example. Like I told you, I was calling Tommy at all hours of the night, and I really chewed Jimmy out over that pallet jack. And Jimmy, he’s a good guy, he’s been with the company for... gosh, it’s got to be fifteen years now. Started out sweeping the loading dock and worked his way up. He’s got two kids in high school, so I know he needs the job, and I did feel a little bad about yelling at him the way I did. I really let him have it, up one side and down the other. But did it cause a serious problem? Not really. He actually brought me a coffee the next week—one of those awful motor oil ones—and we smoothed it over. He knows how the stress gets when the quotas are tight. And as for the work itself, we actually got that big Detroit order out on time. Beat the deadline by half a shift, actually. The front office was thrilled, even if the guys on the floor were probably calling me every name in the book behind my back. So at work... no, no real damage done.

And at home... well, my wife, she’s an absolute saint. Thirty-two years we’ve been married this October. She’s used to me being a bit bullheaded. When I was out there tearing up the deck boards at six in the morning with that crowbar, yeah, she was standing there on the porch in her pink terrycloth bathrobe just shaking her head at me. She told me I was acting like a damn fool and to keep the noise down before the Hendersons next door called the cops on us. But we didn't get into a big blowout fight over it or anything. She just sighed and went back inside to make breakfast. 

And my daughter, like I said, she was just so dialed into that military packing list, she barely even noticed I was acting any different. She was in her own world with the duffel bags. 

So... no. I wouldn't say there were any serious problems. It was a chaotic week, sure, and I was definitely running everybody a little ragged, myself included. I mean, half that deck is still torn up right now, just sitting under a blue plastic tarp because I ran out of steam on it. But we all just kind of got through it. I didn't ruin anything or break anything that can't be fixed, if that's what you're asking.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior elevated/irritable episode caused marked impairment requiring consequences beyond interpersonal friction, which would support mania over hypomania and separate bipolar I from bipolar II/depressive disorders.
doctor.question: During that fired-up period, were you hospitalized or forced to stop working because of how you were acting?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the elevated mood period caused hospitalization or forced the patient to stop working (assessing for manic vs. hypomanic severity). The patient's functional_impairment profile only describes impairment during the current depressive episode, not the fired-up period.

patient.answer:
Hospitalized? Oh, Lord, no. No, no, no. I haven't been in a hospital since... well, since my wife had our girl, and obviously I was just there pacing the waiting room for that one. I really don't hold with hospitals unless you've got a bone sticking out of your leg or you're bleeding out, you know? And even then, I'd probably just try to wrap it up with some duct tape and finish my shift. 

And forced to stop working? Doc, I don't think you quite get how things run down at the plant. If I stop working, the whole operation goes belly up. I'm the guy keeping all those plates spinning. Like I was saying about that big Detroit order... if I had just up and walked out, or if the front office had come down and told me to take a hike because I was acting too fired up, we would have missed that shipping deadline. Period. And if we lose that account, then guys like Jimmy are out of a job, and I'm not about to let that happen. 

I've been working since I was a kid, you know. Left school back in the eighth grade to pull my weight for my folks, and I haven't stopped grinding since. It's just what you do. You don't stop working just because your motor's running a little hot or you've got a lot of ideas buzzing around. Heck, management probably loved that I was pushing the line so hard, even if I was being a real pain in the neck to be around. So, no. Nobody forced me to clock out, and I definitely didn't end up in any hospital bed. I was right there on the factory floor, every single day, usually before the sun even came up. I don't even have the time to be sick, let alone lay around in a hospital somewhere.

target_item.manifestation: I got it in my head that I was about to be regional director and that nobody in the company understood operations like I did, even though I don't usually talk that big.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient felt more confident or capable than usual during the fired-up spell, which directly maps to inflated self-esteem or grandiosity.

patient.answer:
Confident? Well... yeah. Yeah, confident doesn't even really begin to cover it, doc. It was more like... I felt like I was ten feet tall and bulletproof. 

See, normally, you know, I’m a nose-to-the-grindstone kind of guy. I keep my head down, I get the product out the door, and I go home. I'm not a bragger. I really don't usually talk that big or toot my own horn. I just let the work speak for itself. But during that stretch with the Detroit order? Man, I... I got it in my head that I was about to be made regional director. 

I mean, just think about that for a second. The regional director, Mr. Gable, he’s got some fancy business degree, wears a suit and tie every day, sits in an air-conditioned office in Chicago. And here I am, a guy who left school in the eighth grade, with grease on my boots. But that week, I didn't care about any of that. I was absolutely convinced that the big bosses were going to come down, fire Gable, and put me in charge of the whole Midwest division. 

I was walking around the floor telling anybody who would listen—Tommy, Jimmy, Brenda up at the front desk—that nobody in the entire company understood operations like I did. Nobody. I was looking at the way corporate had the shipping manifests organized and I was just laughing out loud, telling the guys how stupid the suits were and how I was gonna fix the whole supply chain the second I got my big promotion. I felt like I had this... this special insight, you know? Like my brain was running on high-octane gas and everybody else was just pedaling a tricycle. 

I even went home and told my wife we were going to need to start looking at nicer cars, maybe a Cadillac or a Lincoln, because I was going to be doing a lot of driving between all the different plants I'd be running. She tried to tell me to slow down, asked me if I'd actually talked to anybody in management about this, but I just waved her off. I told her they’d be coming to me any day now. I just felt like I was the only guy in the whole state who actually knew how to run things. It’s a little embarrassing to think about now, to be honest with you, because like I said, I don't usually act like I'm God's gift to manufacturing. But right then? I really believed I was the smartest guy in the room.
